title: Classes in depth
lesson:
In Level 1 you wrote `static` methods: a name, some parameters, a result. That works until your data starts to have a **life**. A water tank has a level that goes up and down. A savings group member has a balance that changes every week. A **class** bundles that data (fields) with the methods that are allowed to change it. Each `new WaterTank(500)` is an **object**: its own copy of the fields.

**Constructors** run once, when the object is made. They are the one place to make sure an object starts in a good state:

```
public WaterTank(double capacity) {
    if (capacity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be positive");
    this.capacity = capacity;
}
```

`this` means "the object being built or used". `this.capacity = capacity` copies the parameter into the field with the same name. You can also have several constructors (**overloading**), and one can call another with `this(...)` as its first line, so the checks live in one place.

**Encapsulation**: make fields `private` and give only the methods that make sense (`fill`, `use`, `getLevel`). Then nobody can write `tank.level = -40` from outside. Every change goes through a method that checks it. This is the main reason classes exist: the object protects its own rules, so the rest of the program can trust it.

**static vs instance.** An instance field belongs to one object (each tank has its own level). A `static` field belongs to the class, shared by all objects: a counter of how many tickets were issued, a constant like `MAX_LEVEL`. A static method can't see instance fields, because it isn't called on any particular object.

The common mistakes:
- Forgetting `this.` so `capacity = capacity;` assigns the parameter to itself. The field stays 0.
- Public fields "to save time". Then a bug anywhere can break the object, and you can't find who did it.
- Putting a counter in an instance field: every object gets its own counter, so every ticket is number 1.

In games, every enemy, bullet and pickup is an object with private state. In robotics, a `Motor` class refuses speeds outside its safe range. The habit is the same: **validate in the constructor and in every method that changes state**.

notes: `made` is static: one number for the whole class, counting every tank.
`capacity` is final: set once in the constructor, never changed.
The constructor refuses a bad capacity, so every Tank starts valid.
`Tank()` calls `this(1000)`: the second constructor reuses the first one's checks.
Fields are private; the outside world uses getLevel() and fill().

exercises.title: A safe water tank
exercises.prompt: Finish class WaterTank. Constructor WaterTank(double capacity): throw IllegalArgumentException if capacity <= 0; the level starts at 0. getCapacity() and getLevel() return the fields. fill(double litres) adds water but never above capacity and returns how much actually went in; negative litres throw IllegalArgumentException. use(double litres) takes water out and returns true, or returns false and changes nothing if there isn't enough; negative litres throw IllegalArgumentException. percentFull() returns the level as a percent of capacity rounded to 1 decimal (Math.round(x * 10) / 10.0).

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { WaterTank t = new WaterTank(500); t.fill(200); return t.getLevel() + ""; }).get()
tests.name: fill adds water

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { WaterTank t = new WaterTank(500); t.fill(200); return t.fill(400) + " " + t.getLevel(); }).get()
tests.name: fill stops at capacity

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { WaterTank t = new WaterTank(100); t.fill(30); return t.use(50) + " " + t.use(20) + " " + t.getLevel(); }).get()
tests.name: use

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { WaterTank t = new WaterTank(300); t.fill(100); return t.percentFull() + ""; }).get()
tests.name: percentFull
zero capacity
tests.hint_if_fail: Check capacity <= 0 in the constructor and throw.

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { WaterTank t = new WaterTank(50); t.fill(-5); return "no error"; }).get()
tests.name: negative fill

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { WaterTank t = new WaterTank(50); t.use(-1); return "no error"; }).get()
tests.name: negative use

hints: The amount that fits is capacity - level. Add Math.min(litres, capacity - level).
In use(): if (litres > level) return false; before changing anything.
Validate first, then change the field: if (litres < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative");

exercises.title: Savings group member
exercises.prompt: Class Member for a savings group. Member(String name, double savings): the name is trimmed; a blank name or negative savings throws IllegalArgumentException. Member(String name) starts with 0 savings and must call the other constructor with this(...). getName(), getSavings(). deposit(double amount) adds to the savings; amount <= 0 throws IllegalArgumentException. describe() returns e.g. "Amina: 1500.0 KSh".

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { Member m = new Member("Otieno", 200); m.deposit(50.5); return m.getSavings() + ""; }).get()
tests.name: deposit
blank name
tests.hint_if_fail: name.isBlank() is true for spaces only.

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { Member m = new Member("Akinyi"); m.deposit(0); return "no error"; }).get()
tests.name: deposit of 0

tests.why: Member(String name) should call the other constructor: this(name, 0);

hints: The one-argument constructor is a single line: this(name, 0);
Put all the checks in the two-argument constructor, before assigning: if (name == null || name.isBlank()) throw ...

exercises.title: Clinic queue tickets
exercises.prompt: Each new Ticket(String patient) gets the next number: 1, 2, 3... The starter keeps the counter in an instance field, so every ticket is number 1. Fix it with a static counter. getNumber(), getPatient(), label() gives "#3 Otieno". static issued() returns how many tickets were made since the last reset; static reset() starts counting from 1 again.

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { Ticket.reset(); new Ticket("Amina"); new Ticket("Juma"); return new Ticket("Otieno").label(); }).get()
tests.name: numbers go up

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { Ticket.reset(); new Ticket("A"); new Ticket("B"); return Ticket.issued() + ""; }).get()
tests.name: issued

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { Ticket.reset(); new Ticket("A"); Ticket.reset(); return new Ticket("Amina").label() + " " + Ticket.issued(); }).get()
tests.name: reset starts again

hints: Make the counter static: private static int nextNumber = 1;
issued() is nextNumber - 1; reset() sets nextNumber = 1.

quiz.q: In a constructor, you write `capacity = capacity;` (no `this.`). What happens?
choices: The parameter is assigned to itself and the field stays 0
quiz.why: The parameter hides the field; use this.capacity = capacity.

quiz.q: Why make the level field private?
choices: So every change goes through methods that check it
quiz.why: Encapsulation: the object protects its own rules.

quiz.q: A static field `count` in class Enemy is…
quiz.why: static belongs to the class, not to an object.

quiz.q: Which line correctly calls another constructor of the same class?
quiz.why: this(...) must be the first statement.

quiz.q: A static method tries to read an instance field `level`. Result?
choices: Compile error: no object to read it from
Works if the field is private
quiz.why: Static methods aren't called on an object.

cards.q: What does `this` mean inside a method?
cards.a: The object the method was called on (or is being built).
In the constructor and in every method that changes state.
static: one for the whole class. instance: one per object.
this(...) as the first line calls another constructor of the same class.

explain: Explain encapsulation in your own words, using an example object you make up (a tank, a bank account, a game character): what goes wrong without it?
